summary:
Guam stands under the United States framework as an unincorporated territory of the United States. Federal hate crime protection for gender identity has applied in Guam since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act.

Same-sex marriage has been lawful in Guam since June 2015. Chief Judge Frances M. Tydingco-Gatewood struck down the prohibition on 5 June 2015 in a case brought after Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero were denied a licence in April 2015, with the ruling effective at 8 a.m. on 9 June 2015. Licences were issued four days after the ruling, and the Guam Marriage Equality Act of 2015, passed on 11 August 2015, made marriage laws gender neutral. The ruling cited Latta v. Otter.

Airport screening in Guam follows Transportation Security Administration procedure, which applies in Guam as a United States territory. Body scanner and pat down procedures can disclose a transgender traveller's status to officers. Travellers may request alternative screening and may escalate problems on the spot. Guidance addresses pre flight packing and document and screening mismatches, and most transgender travellers pass screening without incident.

Guam is described as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment. That description is framed for LGBTQ people generally rather than for transgender people specifically.
tangentialFactors:
A January 2025 executive order prohibits transgender troops from serving openly and directs Secretary of Defense Hegseth to submit an implementation plan within 30 days. The order describes transgender identity as radical gender ideology. It applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent United States military presence.

Private adult consensual and non commercial homosexual acts have been lawful in Guam since reform of the Criminal Code in 1978. The prior 1933 penal code, ordained by the Naval Governor and identical to California law, prohibited sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus whether heterosexual or homosexual with one to ten years imprisonment. The only reported sodomy case in the early 1950s, Pennington v. Government, resulted in victory for the defendant solely on procedural grounds that the trial court lacked authority to try him without a jury.

Guam became the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage under the June 2015 ruling.

The inventory states that the Chamorro people have traditionally accepted homosexuality and transgender people. It describes historic Chamorro society as a very sexually tolerant society where homosexuality was never viewed as taboo but was taken for granted as part of life, without giving a separate historic account specific to transgender people beyond the statement of acceptance.

Since the 1990s Guam has had a visible LGBTQ social scene with a handful of nightclubs and locally organized social functions. Guam Pride has been held annually since 2017 and attracts a few hundred people. Guam is a member of the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association and has begun commercializing itself as a tourist destination for LGBTQ people.
localsOnly:
Guam permits legal gender change only after sex reassignment surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a transgender applicant must provide the Office of Vital Statistics with a sworn physician statement that sex reassignment surgery has been undergone, after which the Office amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended driver's license upon receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed.

In May 2018 Senator Fernando Esteves introduced a bill to allow legal gender change without surgery through judicial permission plus a letter confirming gender identity with documentation from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional affirming that the request reflects the applicant's sex or gender identity. The Legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 until medical and law enforcement process issues were addressed, then defeated the bill on 17 December 2018 by six votes to seven.

Employment discrimination based on gender identity or expression is prohibited under Bill 102-33, passed unanimously in August 2015, including discrimination against government employees based on identity.

Following marriage legalization, adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted and lesbian couples have access to assisted reproduction such as in vitro fertilization. Guam recognizes the non genetic non gestational parent as legal parent through donor insemination only if married, and the Department of Public Health and Social Services has entered both spouses on birth certificates of children with same-sex parents since May 2017.
